Hi Elena / Dan — Karthik here from Infra. Below are concrete answers; I kept them short and included action items at the end.

1) Connectivity options (summary)
- AWS PrivateLink (preferred for hosted customers): we publish an NLB-backed Service Name. Customer creates an Interface Endpoint in their VPC. Traffic to the service goes over AWS private network; no public IPs traverse the internet. After you create the endpoint we will provide the NLB ENI IPs (typically within your VPC’s AZs) if you need to inspect.
- Azure Private Endpoint: we expose a Private Link Service; customer creates a Private Endpoint and approves our service. DNS requires a private A record for the endpoint; we'll provide the FQDN to add to your resolvers.
- GCP (VPC peering / Private Service Connect): we can support Private Service Connect for tighter isolation. VPC peering for dedicated/on-prem contracts is available but requires route table changes on both sides.

2) IP allowlist / public egress ranges
- For customers that cannot use PrivateLink, we publish a stable set of egress IP ranges used by the hosted API. We attach the CSV (ip-ranges-2026-04.csv). Current publish snapshot (examples):
  - 34.201.128.0/18
  - 52.55.128.0/17
  - 13.225.64.0/18
(See attached CSV for the full list and region mapping. We update these quarterly; changes are communicated 30 days in advance.)

3) Required security group / route table rules (customer side)
- PrivateLink:
  - Security groups on the interface endpoint: allow inbound TCP 443 from your app subnets (or specific CIDRs).
  - No additional NAT egress rules required because traffic stays inside AWS backbone.
- VPC peering (GCP/AWS):
  - Add route table entries for our service CIDR into your VPC route table.
  - Ensure SGs/NACLs allow TCP 443 from your application subnets.
- Public egress option:
  - Allow outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) to the published egress CIDRs. Some customers also allow ephemeral ports for specific workflows — see action item below.

4) TLS / mTLS
- Hosted (public API): server-side TLS (TLS 1.2/1.3) is standard. mTLS is not enabled by default for the hosted public API.
- Private/Dedicated deployments: we support customer-provided mTLS (client certs) for API traffic — common for regulated workloads. For PrivateLink interfaces, mTLS can be enabled on Dedicated plans where we control the load-balancer configuration.

Action items / timeline
- I will attach a short network diagram (redwood-sig-network-arch-diagram.png) and the ip-ranges-2026-04.csv in this thread.
- If you pick PrivateLink, we can generate the service name and provision NLB mappings after contract signature; NLB IPs are typically available in T+2 business days after provisioning.
- If you prefer the public allowlist approach, please confirm which regions you need so we can provide region-scoped CIDRs.

If you'd like, we can run a short 30-minute walk-through and provision a sandbox endpoint for testing.

Thanks,

Elena — quick final notes following the walkthrough and our internal checklist:

- NLB IP stability: confirmed — NLB ENI IPs are stable for the lifetime of that NLB. They may change if we reprovision the service (rare) or when moving between instance types/major infra events. We'll annotate the diagram text exactly as Hannah suggested.
- CSV integrity: the ip-ranges CSV is published on our secure Drive and we provide a SHA256 hash with each quarterly snapshot. We can also provide ASN metadata on request.
- mTLS: confirmed — mTLS is available on Dedicated/Private deployments and for PrivateLink when provisioned under a Dedicated plan. Hosted public API does not currently support client cert auth.
- Sandbox provisioning timeline: if you want a sandbox PrivateLink endpoint for testing, we can create a service name and NLB in T+2 business days after you confirm the test contract. If you go the public-allowlist route, we'll provide region-scoped CSV rows within 1 business day.

Checklist for your infra team to review before the cutover:
- Decide between PrivateLink (recommended) vs public egress allowlist.
- If PrivateLink: approve service name and create an Interface Endpoint; ensure SGs allow TCP 443 inbound from your app subnets.
- If public allowlist: add the published CIDRs to your firewall/allowlist and allow outbound TCP 443. Optionally allow ephemeral ports for specific flows — let us know if you need those opened.

I'll attach the SHA256 for the current CSV to the Drive folder. If you need signed attestation for SOC2 artifacts beyond the summary file, please raise a ticket (SEC-412) and our compliance team will coordinate.
